source.title: The 9 Unsolved Mysteries Mathematicians Can’t Stop Thinking About

accepted.question_text: Does there exist an odd perfect number, where a perfect number means a positive integer equal to the sum of its proper factors? Equivalently, is there any odd positive integer with the same property illustrated by even examples such as 6 = 3 + 2 + 1 and 28 = 14 + 7 + 4 + 2 + 1?

evidence.quote: My favorite problem is also the oldest-known problem in math: Are there odd perfect numbers? A perfect number is the sum of its proper factors such as 6 = 3 + 2 + 1 or 28 = 14 + 7 + 4 + 2 + 1. All known perfect numbers are even.

accepted.question_text: Is there an efficient general algorithm that, given an integer n known to be the product of two prime numbers p and q and given n in ordinary notation, recovers the factors p and q with running time that grows only modestly with the number of digits of n, rather than exponentially as in trial division and related known methods?

evidence.page: Section "How Efficiently Can we Factor Integers?"
evidence.quote: If I write out n for you (in decimal notation, say), how can you recover p and q? What is an efficient general algorithm for this task that you could program in a computer? (By “efficient,” we mean that the run time of the algorithm should grow modestly with the size of n, say linearly or quadratically with the number of digits.)

accepted.question_text: Is the Kummer-Vandiver conjecture true: for every odd prime number p, does p fail to divide the class number of the maximal real subfield of the p-th cyclotomic field, that is, the number system obtained by adjoining a p-th root of 1 to the rational numbers and then taking its maximal real subfield?

evidence.quote: In the mid 1800s, Ernst Kummer first conjectured in letters to Leopold Kronecker that for any odd prime number p, the prime p does not divide the class number of the maximal real subfield of the p-th cyclotomic field—in other words, the number system we get when we adjoin a p-th root of 1 to the rational numbers.

accepted.question_text: Given an algebraic variety over the complex numbers, how can one construct interesting algebraic subvarieties of that variety? In the specific open case highlighted here, the generalized Hodge conjecture predicts many interesting surfaces inside hypersurfaces of degree d defined by one degree-d equation in projective space of dimension at least 2d; is that prediction true for general d beyond the very small values already understood?

evidence.page: Section "How To Construct Interesting Algebraic Subvarieties"
evidence.quote: The most important question we are faced with is: How do we construct interesting algebraic subvarieties of a given algebraic variety?

evidence.page: Section "How To Construct Interesting Algebraic Subvarieties"
evidence.quote: For example, the generalized Hodge conjecture predicts the existence of a lot of interesting surfaces in hypersurfaces of degree d, defined by a single degree d equation in projective space of dimension at least 2d. This small special case, which can be stated without appealing to any notion of topology, is completely open except for very small values of d.

accepted.question_text: Can one construct a general computer algorithm that takes as input an algebraic equation f(x,y) = 0 and outputs all of its rational solutions? The problem asks for a uniform procedure for arbitrary Diophantine equations of this kind, not merely for isolated examples or restricted families, even though many such equations are believed or known to have only finitely many rational solutions.

evidence.page: Section "Even after Thousands of Years of Study, Diophantine Equations are Extremely Hard"
evidence.quote: Construct a computer algorithm that takes any such equation as input and writes down all the rational solutions:

evidence.page: Section "Even after Thousands of Years of Study, Diophantine Equations are Extremely Hard"
evidence.quote: The key challenge, then, is to construct such a DE algorithm, which sounds simple but turns out to be ridiculously difficult.

accepted.question_text: Which quadruples of integers (v, e, s, f) can occur as the numbers of vertices, edges, two-dimensional sides, and three-dimensional facets of a four-dimensional polyhedron? More specifically, what is the complete set of necessary and sufficient conditions characterizing the face-number data of 4D polyhedra, beyond the currently known relations such as v - e + s - f = 0, lower bounds v >= 5 and f >= 5, and inequalities like 2e >= 4v and 2s >= 4f?

evidence.page: Section "How Many Faces Can a Four-Dimensional Polyhedron Have?"
evidence.quote: Four-dimensional polyhedra have vertices, edges and two-dimensional sides. They also have 3D sides; I’ll call these facets. How many of each can a 4D polyhedron have?

evidence.page: Section "How Many Faces Can a Four-Dimensional Polyhedron Have?"
evidence.quote: But we don’t know the complete set. I can give a set of integers that satisfy all the conditions we know but for which there is no 4D polyhedron. And we don’t even have a guess for what the complete set of conditions is.

accepted.question_text: Is the Heil-Ramanathan-Topiwala (HRT) conjecture true: for every nonzero square-integrable function on the real line, is every finite set of its time-frequency shifts linearly independent? Here a time-frequency shift is obtained by translating the function by a real parameter p and multiplying the result by a complex exponential of frequency q.

evidence.quote: They stated that any finite set of time-frequency shifts of a nonzero, square-integrable function on the real line is linearly independent.
The conjecture remains unproven, however, even when dealing with an arbitrary nonzero square-integrable function and any arbitrary set of four distinct points in the plane.

accepted.question_text: Does every smoothly embedded 3-dimensional sphere in 4-dimensional space bound a ball? More generally, the article frames this as the Schoenflies problem for smooth spheres in codimension one, and reports that the remaining open case is precisely the case of smooth 3D spheres sitting inside 4D space.

evidence.quote: Does a smooth sphere in space bound a ball? This is known as the Schoenflies problem.
But the question remains open for smooth 3D spheres in 4D space.

accepted.question_text: How far can knots in arbitrary three-manifolds be from knots in ordinary 3-dimensional space, when distance is measured by the complexity of a surface connecting one knot to the other? In particular, beyond specially constructed examples, what bounds or classifications describe this distance for arbitrary knots in three-manifolds?

evidence.quote: One question that really interests me is how far away knots in other three-manifolds can be from knots in 3D space.
At the same time, a lot of those knots were specifically constructed for our techniques to work, and we have a lot to learn to answer that question for arbitrary knots.
